correctness.summary: An exact spectral-moment identity for each symmetric GMRES(1) step, combined with a scalar sum-of-squares certificate, proves the squared Euclidean solution-error ratio is at most 4/3. A two-eigenvalue indefinite construction attains equality and forms an exact two-step directional cycle. Separate moment, two-point, and nonsymmetric calculations verify the definite monotonicity, absence of a nontrivial absolute-condition-number safety window, and necessity of symmetry.

originality.scope: to the best of our knowledge
originality.summary: Classical and recent literature establishes residual minimization, qualitative residual/error mismatch, error estimators, and sharp residual convergence factors for GMRES(1). Searches under GMRES(1), MRI, Orthomin(1), minimal discrepancy, solution-error amplification and exact constant/equality formulations did not locate the 2/sqrt(3) Euclidean solution-error barrier, its equality classification, or the exact alternating equality cycle. Older minimum-error/minimum-residual literature remains a material historical-equivalence risk.

value.summary: The result gives a sharp dimension-free cap on how far residual minimization can move the Euclidean solution error in the wrong direction for symmetric systems, together with a recurring equality example, a definite/indefinite dichotomy, and a sharp contrast with unbounded nonsymmetric amplification.

limitations: Exact arithmetic, real symmetric nonsingular matrices and the ordinary Euclidean norm only.
The iteration is MRI/GMRES(1), restarted after every one-dimensional Krylov correction; the bound is not asserted for consecutive full-MINRES or full-GMRES iterates.
The per-cycle bound does not imply global convergence on symmetric indefinite systems, where GMRES(1) may stagnate.
Arbitrary preconditioning, finite-precision effects and nonsymmetric matrices are outside the theorem; nonsymmetric one-step error amplification can be unbounded.
Older minimum-residual and minimum-error literature, especially Fridman (1963) and Saad (2000), leaves residual originality risk because complete theorem-level checking was not available.
Independent audit has not been performed.
